extracted.intended_audience: landscape painters, art students, and art critics studying Turner's handling of water and foliage
extracted.subtask_description: Practical and critical guidance for representing running water (torrents, rivers, breakers, open sea) and vegetation in landscape painting, emphasizing truthful drawing of form, motion, mass, foam, and tree-structure. Draws examples and standards from Turner's works (Llanthony Abbey, Mercury and Argus, Land's End, Slave Ship, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Curved lines of the continuous torrent
rubrics_metrics.description: When water has gained an impetus it 'takes the shape of its bed', forming long undulating curved lines (convex to concave) that express extreme power and velocity; the undulating line is the exclusive attribute of the mountain-torrent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Render continuous torrents with sweeping, united curves that follow every swell and hollow of the bed; avoid breaking these into scattered bright touches. Use studied chiaroscuro and delicate color (grays and greens) to draw each fine form. Exemplars: Llanthony Abbey (standard of torrent-drawing), the lower fall of the Tees, Killiecrankie, Rhymer's Glen.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interrupted torrent (leaps, pools, ripples)
rubrics_metrics.description: Some streams resolve into repeated leaps into pools and glassy basins; their character is 'interrupted' with cascades, tinkling threads, concentric ripples, and localized sparkling foam.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Record each phase and phenomenon exactly where it is most valuable to the impression: show reflective pools, trickling threads through leaves, curdling ripples around stones, and foam over basin-lips. Example: Mercury and Argus—use of quiet pools and three cascades to convey repose and localized motion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Binary classification of running water
rubrics_metrics.description: All drawing of running water will resolve into representation of one or other of two great divisions: the continuous torrent and the interrupted torrent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide which class a subject belongs to early and compose the drawing accordingly; the methods and line-work appropriate to each class differ fundamentally (see continuous vs interrupted criteria).

rubrics_metrics.name: Sea must be legitimately drawn; express weight and mass
rubrics_metrics.description: Sea-painting cannot be faked by dexterities; the weight, mass, and organization of the sea must be legitimately expressed—failure to do so yields conventional or lifeless results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim to convey the mass, unity, and internal organization of the sea (broad swells, furrows of swell, groupings of breakers) rather than relying on superficial white touches. Partial successes are praiseworthy; true success requires great power of drawing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Foam: two invariable conditions to consider
rubrics_metrics.description: On breaking waves two foam-conditions invariable occur: (1) the thick creamy curdling overlapping mass which exists for a moment after the fall and in shore run-up, and (2) the thin white coating with oval gaps and clefts that marbles the surface and connects breakers by long dragging streams.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Both forms are extremely difficult to render: the former requires delicate gradations of high light and cast shadow along projecting 'lips'; the latter involves complex oval openings seen in undulation and perspective. Be aware that many attempts omit or misrepresent these; conventionalisms often substitute deceptive tricks for legitimate rendering.

rubrics_metrics.name: Breakers on an even shore: formal curve plus top laxity and wind effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Shore-breakers combine mathematical purity in their hollow curved surface (parallel lines, graduated reflected/transmitted lights) with a sudden laxity at the lip where the water 'gives way' and the wind acts on the edge, producing forms projected by weight and forms blown away.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Depict the precise, flat curvature of the wave body, then show a contrasting lax, chain-like motion at the crest and variable spray where wind intervenes. The final crash at the shore is especially hard to render; attempts often lack 'thunder'—accept limits and use composed aids (e.g., figures, cables) to convey force where pure foam will not suffice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Viewer position alters the impression of sea motion
rubrics_metrics.description: The impression of the sea differs radically when seen from the shore versus afloat: from shore waves appear successive and similar; afloat the same water seems to rise, crash, recoil, and change perpetually, revealing a perturbed, unwearied spirit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To convey grand characters of the sea (fitfulness, power, recoil), place the spectator off the shore (20–30 yards out) in composition where feasible (examples: Land's End, Fowey, Dunbar, Laugharne). Choose viewpoint deliberately to achieve the desired impression of the water's life.

rubrics_metrics.name: Flat, sweeping lines and expression of weight for rolling sea
rubrics_metrics.description: Size and sublimity arise from the breadth of masses and the flatness of lines rather than mere height; Turner's rolling sea shows surges that 'roll and plunge' with prostration and weight, little broken by wind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a few dark continuous furrows of swell to divide space and indicate enormous mass; emphasize breadth and flatness of line, minimal breaking by wind (only a fringe of torn spray), and undulating lines where waves meet rocks to show immense weight and force.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recoiling waves and vertical bounds
rubrics_metrics.description: When a breaking surge is hurled against a vertical rock or the recoil of a preceding wave, it may be dashed back and meet following breakers to produce vertical bounds—large vertical fountains or leaps.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Represent these encounters to inform viewers about coast nature and force; examples: Land's End, Quilleboeuf, vignette to Lycidas. Show the report-like blow and the resultant vertical fountain where applicable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Depict the sea after prolonged storm (yesty foam, loss of horizon)
rubrics_metrics.description: After prolonged gales the sea exhibits 'yesty' whipped foam in ropes and wreaths, masses half water half air torn into spray, and mist so thick that horizon and landmarks are annihilated—the sea and air become indistinguishable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Convey the choking spray, ropes of foam carried by wind, low rain-clouds mingling with spray, and the loss of horizon. This state is unusual and often incomprehensible to most viewers; when depicted (e.g., Snowstorm), expect difficulty of comprehension and prepare strong, truthful effects of mist and light.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity of truth, color, drawing, tone, and composition (ideal grounded in truth)
rubrics_metrics.description: A great sea-picture (exemplified by the Slave Ship) combines daring, ideal conception with concentrated truthful knowledge: perfect color modulation, fearless accurate drawing, true tones, buoyant motion, and unified composition dedicated to a sublime subject.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compose works so that each square inch contributes to the whole; ground imaginative or ideal elements in observed truth and technical mastery. Strive for unity: color not false or morbid, drawing accurate, and tones harmonized to support the subject's meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer accurate contours and drawing over deceptive tricks
rubrics_metrics.description: The real contours of water and its sweeping forms ought to be drawn even at the cost of some loss of color, freedom, or brightness; many scratching/dashing tricks produce deceptive resemblance but sacrifice sublimity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize determined, laborious rendering of contour to secure grandeur. It is often better that a drawing 'miss of being like water' than that it miss the grandeur of water by relying on trick touches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choice of representation (reflections vs surface for repose)
rubrics_metrics.description: An artist may lawfully choose different adaptations of sight (e.g., giving clear reflections to suggest depth, or losing surface reflections to suggest repose); either choice may be legitimate depending on the desired effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide intentionally whether to render clear distant reflections or to compress surface and lose depth to obtain power or repose. Use such choices to serve the picture's effect rather than slavishly copying all observed phenomena.

rubrics_metrics.name: Laws of forest trees: branches divide, not taper
rubrics_metrics.description: For ordinary European forest/copse trees (oak, elm, ash, beech, etc.), stems and boughs do not taper except at a fork; when a stem sends off a branch the original piece becomes less in diameter by exactly the quantity sent off and then remains the same diameter until the next fork.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Paint tree structure with branch diameters conserved across divisions so that, if all twigs were united, they would form a round log as large as the trunk. Do not render branches thinning continuously toward tips; render division and mass correctly to achieve truthful foliage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Record phenomena where they are most valuable to the impression
rubrics_metrics.description: Each phase or phenomenon of nature (wave-form, pool, ripple, spray, reflection) should be recorded exactly where it contributes most to the impression of the work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compose selectively: include those particulars of motion, light, or form that enhance the intended expression (e.g., use a jet of spray or a tossed cable to help express force). Avoid adding details that distract from the unified truth of the scene.
